e-4816.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection
e-4816.problem: Consider the vectors ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/308390111ffcb243fb8612b873317302c966df288001b28c6d9b02f5946aac94.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/a7df5d5b19c15a0e5f7b9d1dc93d810ca41b70c84d28c770a0d15521b14d1374.png) Find a basis of $S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}$ by inspection.
e-4816.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that $\mathbf{a}_2$ is a linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{a}_2=1\cdot \mathbf{a}_1+1\cdot \mathbf{a}_3
$$

Consequently, the vector $\mathbf{a}_2$ can be removed from $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}$ without changing the span. So $S = \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}$ is spanned by just $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\}.$ 

Lastly, note that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\},$ that is to say,

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/e13b964d4391f86125a17302c70af51040c331eb76393ebb39a1fef65dab569d.png)

e-6237.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns
e-6237.problem: Consider the vectors ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/ea1fe153d54f6a769e3d13177bfede1eb467525feb255fbcfd7ec88efe58b733.png) ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/075599a7512d1105b9c6ad3acf3f4d043cb60c2aedeb8f53532045390c29f1e9.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/73b2b16a58acd290d040047339b0db3c79de19c0af04303e010a2d16e75bb94b.png) Find a basis of $S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$
e-6237.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 15 \\ 2 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ that is to say, 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/c5383ad51988564756ba754cbd6107f487fd0b32be0013f8a89bb78a6900f540.png)

e-6257.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of a Span
e-6257.problem:
The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,$ $\mathbf{a}_2,$ $\mathbf{a}_3,$ and $\mathbf{a}_4$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3, \mathbf{a}_4 \}.$ If that is the case, find $x_1 + x_2 + x_3,$ where $\mathbf{a}_4=x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2+x_3\mathbf{a}_3.$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/1d282bb39042b44ed346503f3c7c4213b02089bbc7d833e82a5d95eb49f4db28.png)
e-6257.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3,\mathbf{a}_4 \}.$ So, we want to find $x_1, x_2, x_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/a23531cb53a9b53f47d8a7080af7de78e6d7cdd7fa3a3632c37a720c7e8ba92c.png)

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=2 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=-2 \\ -3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & -2 \\ -3 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3,\mathbf{a}_4 \}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that $x_1=-5,$ $x_2=0,$ and $x_3=7,$ meaning that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14064318/assets/ca123e2e8451fab6c7b106a5d1a05d153020854c694ec41cfb5d38de2fb3ae5f.png)

Therefore, $x_1 + x_2 +  x_3 = (-5) + 0 + 7 = 2.$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ by inspection.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{2}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
{a}_{2}=2\cdot {a}_{1}+0\cdot {a}_{3}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{2}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}}.
$$

after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=1\cdot {a}_{1}+1\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}}.
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the vectors a1=[−30],a2=[25], and a3=[−15]. Find a basis of S=Span{a1,a2,a3} by inspection.

a
 B={[−30],[25],[−15]}
b
 B={[−15]}
c
 B={[25]}
d
 B={[−30],[25]}
e
 B={[−30]}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Remember that a basis of S is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans S.

From the given vectors, we can see that a3 is a linear combination of vectors a1 and a2:

a3=1⋅a1+1⋅a2

Consequently, the vector a3 can be removed from Span{a1,a2,a3} without changing the span. So S=Span{a1,a2,a3} is spanned by just {a1,a2}.

Lastly, note that a1 and a2 are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set {a1,a2} is a linearly independent set that spans S.

Therefore, a basis of S is {a1,a2}, that is to say,

B={[−30]⏟a1,[25]⏟a2}.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d: a₃ = a₁ + a₂, so a₃ is redundant. The vectors a₁ and a₂ are not parallel and therefore form a linearly independent spanning set. Option a is dependent, explaining the incorrect submitted result.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection
content.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
content.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=1\cdot {a}_{1}+1\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}}.
$$

decision.explanation: Since a₃ = −a₂, removing a₃ preserves the span. Vectors a₁ and a₂ are not parallel, so they are linearly independent and form a basis of S.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=0\cdot {a}_{1}+(-1)\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}}.
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the vectors a1=[0−4],a2=[44], and a3=[−4−4]. Find a basis of S=Span{a1,a2,a3} by inspection.

a
B={[0−4],[44],[−4−4]}
b
B={[44]}
c
B={[−4−4],[44]}
d
B={[0−4],[44]}
e
B={[0−4]}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that a basis of S is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans S.

From the given vectors, we can see that a3 is a linear combination of vectors a1 and a2:

a3=0⋅a1+(−1)⋅a2

Consequently, the vector a3 can be removed from Span{a1,a2,a3} without changing the span. So S=Span{a1,a2,a3} is spanned by just {a1,a2}.

Lastly, note that a1 and a2 are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set {a1,a2} is a linearly independent set that spans S.

Therefore, a basis of S is {a1,a2}, that is to say,

B={[0−4]⏟a1,[44]⏟a2}.

content.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=0\cdot {a}_{1}+(-1)\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}}.
$$

decision.explanation: Since a₃ = a₁ + a₂, removing a₃ preserves the span. Vectors a₁ and a₂ are not parallel, so they are linearly independent and form a basis of S.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=1\cdot {a}_{1}+1\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}}.
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the vectors a1=[05],a2=[−22], and a3=[−27]. Find a basis of S=Span{a1,a2,a3} by inspection.

a
 B={[05]}
b
 B={[−22]}
c
 B={[05],[−22]}
d
 B={[05],[−22],[−27]}
e
 B={[−27]}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Remember that a basis of S is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans S.

From the given vectors, we can see that a3 is a linear combination of vectors a1 and a2:

a3=1⋅a1+1⋅a2

Consequently, the vector a3 can be removed from Span{a1,a2,a3} without changing the span. So S=Span{a1,a2,a3} is spanned by just {a1,a2}.

Lastly, note that a1 and a2 are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set {a1,a2} is a linearly independent set that spans S.

Therefore, a basis of S is {a1,a2}, that is to say,

B={[05]⏟a1,[−22]⏟a2}.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c. Since a₃ = a₁ + a₂, removing a₃ preserves the span. Vectors a₁ and a₂ are not parallel, so they form a linearly independent spanning set. Option d is dependent and is not a basis.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection
content.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
content.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=1\cdot {a}_{1}+1\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}}.
$$

decision.explanation: Since a₂ = 2a₁, removing a₂ preserves the span. Vectors a₁ and a₃ are not parallel, so they are linearly independent and form a basis of S.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{2}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
{a}_{2}=2\cdot {a}_{1}+0\cdot {a}_{3}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{2}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}}.
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the vectors a1=[0−2],a2=[0−4], and a3=[1−3]. Find a basis of S=Span{a1,a2,a3} by inspection.

a
B={[1−3]}
b
B={[0−2],[0−4],[1−3]}
c
B={[0−2]}
d
B={[0−2],[1−3]}
e
B={[0−2],[0−4]}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that a basis of S is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans S.

From the given vectors, we can see that a2 is a linear combination of vectors a1 and a3:

a2=2⋅a1+0⋅a3

Consequently, the vector a2 can be removed from Span{a1,a2,a3} without changing the span. So S=Span{a1,a2,a3} is spanned by just {a1,a3}.

Lastly, note that a1 and a3 are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set {a1,a3} is a linearly independent set that spans S.

Therefore, a basis of S is {a1,a3}, that is to say,

B={[0−2]⏟a1,[1−3]⏟a3}.

content.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
content.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{2}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
{a}_{2}=2\cdot {a}_{1}+0\cdot {a}_{3}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{2}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}}.
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the vectors a1=[300],a2=[−200] and a3=[−1−20]. Find a basis B of span{a1,a2,a3}.

a
B={[300],[−1−20]}
b
B={[−1−20]}
c
B={[300],[1−20],[−200]}
d
B={[−200]}
e
B={[300]}
Submit

decision.explanation: Since a₂ = −(2/3)a₁, removing a₂ preserves the span. Vectors a₁ and a₃ are linearly independent: a₃ has a nonzero second coordinate, while a₁ does not. Thus option a is a basis.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.
$$

after.html:
Question 6
?

Consider the vectors a1=[300],a2=[−200] and a3=[−1−20]. Find a basis B of span{a1,a2,a3}.

a
B={[300],[−1−20]}
b
B={[−1−20]}
c
B={[300],[1−20],[−200]}
d
B={[−200]}
e
B={[300]}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

M=[3−2−100−2000]

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the 1st and 3rd columns are pivot columns, while the 2nd column is a non-pivot column.

The 1st and 3rd columns from the original matrix are a1 and a3. So, a basis of S is {a1,a3}, that is to say,

B={[300],[−1−20]}.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a: columns 1 and 3 are pivot columns. Also, a₂ = −(2/3)a₁, while a₁ and a₃ are linearly independent, so {a₁, a₃} is a basis. Option d cannot span a₃.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns
content.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
content.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.
$$

The 1st and 3rd columns from the original matrix are a1 and a3. So, a basis of S is {a1,a3}, that is to say,

B={[300],[−1−20]}.

Your Answer:
B={[−200]}

before.name: Question 7
before.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -9 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$

Consider the vectors a1=[−200], a2=[230], and a3=[−6−90]. Find a basis B of Span{a1,a2,a3}.

decision.explanation: Since a₃ = −3a₂, removing a₃ preserves the span. Vectors a₁ and a₂ are not parallel, so they are linearly independent and form a basis.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -9 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $2$nd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the vectors a1=[−200], a2=[230], and a3=[−6−90]. Find a basis B of Span{a1,a2,a3}.

a
B={[−200]}
b
B={[−6−90]}
c
B={[230],[−6−90]}
d
B={[−200],[230]}
e
B={[230]}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

M=[−22−603−9000]

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the 1st and 2nd columns are pivot columns, while the 3rd column is a non-pivot column.

The 1st and 2nd columns from the original matrix are a1 and a2. So, a basis of S is {a1,a2}, that is to say,

B={[−200],[230]}.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns
content.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -9 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
content.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $2$nd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 16\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & 12 & 6 \\ 4 & 16 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 16 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns

history.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & 12 & 6 \\ 4 & 16 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 16 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}.
$$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the vectors a1=[100],a2=[500], and a3=[620]. Find a basis B of span{a1,a2,a3}.

a
B={[100]}
b
B={[620]}
c
B={[100],[500]}
d
B={[100],[500],[620]}
e
B={[100],[620]}
Submit

decision.explanation: Since a₂ = 5a₁, removing a₂ preserves the span. Vectors a₁ and a₃ are not parallel because a₃ has a nonzero second coordinate. Thus they are linearly independent and form a basis.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.
$$

after.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the vectors a1=[100],a2=[500], and a3=[620]. Find a basis B of span{a1,a2,a3}.

a
B={[100]}
b
B={[620]}
c
B={[100],[500]}
d
B={[100],[500],[620]}
e
B={[100],[620]}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

M=[156002000]

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the 1st and 3rd columns are pivot columns, while the 2nd column is a non-pivot column.

The 1st and 3rd columns from the original matrix are a1 and a3. So, a basis of S is {a1,a3}, that is to say,

B={[100],[620]}.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns
content.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
content.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Consider the vectors a1=[−23], a2=[4−6], and a3=[−2−3]. Find a basis B of Span{a1,a2,a3}.

a
B={[−23]}
b
B={[−23],[−2−3]}
c
B={[−46]}
d
B={[−23],[−46]}
e
B={[−4−6],[−2−3]}
Submit

decision.explanation: Since a₂ = −2a₁, removing a₂ preserves the span. The determinant of columns a₁ and a₃ is (−2)(−3) − (−2)(3) = 12 ≠ 0, so they are linearly independent and form a basis.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the vectors a1=[−23], a2=[4−6], and a3=[−2−3]. Find a basis B of Span{a1,a2,a3}.

a
B={[−23]}
b
B={[−23],[−2−3]}
c
B={[−46]}
d
B={[−23],[−46]}
e
B={[−4−6],[−2−3]}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

A=[−24−23−6−3]R2:=R2+32R1∼[−24−200−6]

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the 1st and 3rd columns are pivot columns, while the 2nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the original matrix, not from the reduced one.

The 1st and 3rd columns from the original matrix are a1 and a3. So, a basis of S is {a1,a3}, that is to say,

B={[−23],[−2−3]}.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns
content.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ ${a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
content.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & -6 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say, 

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}.
$$

a
8
b
−2
c
−6
d

e
−4
Submit

decision.explanation: The determinant of [a₁ a₂] is 2 − 1 = 1, so the vectors are independent. Solving x₁ + x₂ = −6 and x₁ + 2x₂ = −10 gives x₂ = −4 and x₁ = −2. Thus a₃ is in their span, B is a basis, and x₁x₂ = 8.

content.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -10\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that

$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-6 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -6 \\ 1 & 2 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=-4,$ meaning that

$$
(-2)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+(-4)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -10\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-2)\cdot (-4)=8.$

after.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3},$ where ${a}_{4}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{4}=[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -29 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -29 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=-9 \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=-29 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & -9 \\ 3 & 4 & 6 & -29 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-1,$ ${x}_{2}=-2,$ and ${x}_{3}=-3,$ meaning that

$$
(-1)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+(-2)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+(-3)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -29 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=(-1)+(-2)+(-3)=-6.$

Question 13
?

The vectors a1, a2, and a3 are given below. Determine whether B={a1,a2} is a basis of Span{a1,a2,a3}. If that is the case, find x1⋅x2, where a3=x1a1+x2a2. a1=[1−3],a2=[26],a3=[812]

a
3
b
5
c
{a1,a2} is not a basis of Span{a1,a2,a3}
d
2
e
6
Submit

decision.explanation: The determinant of [a₁ a₂] is 6 − 2(−3) = 12 ≠ 0, so the vectors are independent. Solving x₁ + 2x₂ = 8 and −3x₁ + 6x₂ = 12 gives x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3. Thus B is a basis and x₁x₂ = 6.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=8 \\ -3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 12 & 36\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{12}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=3,$ meaning that

$$
2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+3\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of a Span
content.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=8 \\ -3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ -3 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 12 & 36\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{12}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=3,$ meaning that

$$
2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+3\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 3=6.$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 18\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 12\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 18\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2}=-6 \\ 6{x}_{1}+18{x}_{2}=12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 & -6 \\ 6 & 18 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ 6 & 18 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 24\end{aligned}] &  & \end{aligned}
$$

From the second row of the RREF matrix above, we see that the system of equations has no solution.

Therefore, ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is not a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$

The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ where ${a}_{3}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 18\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 12\end{aligned}]
$$

We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R$ such that

$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3},$ where ${a}_{4}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{4}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 5{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-8,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=7,$ meaning that

$$
(-8)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+7\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-8+0+7=-1.$

{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 5{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-8,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=7,$ meaning that

$$
(-8)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+7\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-8+0+7=-1.$
